Scholar Transport Blockade

By: Marion Edmunds | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We find out why the taxi bosses are holding school children to ransom to get transport tenders

Unique Selling Point:
The disconnect between the demands of the local taxi industry in Cape Town, and the desires of the upwardly mobile Khayelitsha community to educate their children is stark. And while the scholar transport blockade can be examined on it's own as a high-stakes contest for power over the provincial transport budget, it is also a symptom of the larger malaise in South Africa, where criminal elements target and extort industries for their own gain, and undermine the rule of law, hastening South Africa's slide to a mafia state. We unpack how the Western Cape government is attempting to block CODETA as it muscles in on a R21 million scholar transport budget. The authorities use the weapons they know how to wield, namely the courts, while CODETA stands it's ground using protest and the threat of violence to make it's point, and gain ground. The school-children, the parents, the teachers and headmasters as well as the businesses who legitimately run kids to and from school are caught in the crossfire.

Summary:
In the week of 13-17th February, taxi bosses flexed their muscles by blockading Khayelitsha so that thousands of children could not get to school on dedicated scholar transport. The following week, the matter is in court for an adjudication of a dispute which the WCED calls extortion, and the taxi association in question, CODETA, believes is a fair form of protest.

While CODETA’s primary target was transport which was running on Western Cape Education tenders, the school blockade also affected local lift clubs, private community-based scholar transport systems that were paid for parents, and parents in private cars trying to get their kids to school.

The numbers of children at home daily last week varied from 5000 to 2500.

This was the biggest blockade but other blockades have been taking place for weeks on a smaller scale in other areas.

CODETA shifted its response on Thursday week back to only the tender-based transport, allowing the minnows through the net. So 2854 learners on four WCED contracted Learner Transport Scheme routes in Khayelitsha had to stay at home. The value of those tenders are R21,7 million and it appears that the main beneficiaries are among others two companies – SWARTZ and ALFREDs.

CODETA spokesperson told me they were not extortionists, but they wanted a piece of the cake. He said the buses were old and unsafe, and the children would be safer transported in taxis. In statements they have called the MEC racist for not engaging with them during the blockade.

• The MEC refused to talk to CODETA while the blockade was ongoing, and took them to court instead, with an urgent interdict on Friday. CODETA and the provincial government signed an agreement endorsed by the court to proceed as follows:

• CODETA will deliver its answering affidavit to the main application by Tuesday.

• The Khayelitsha School Governing Body Association will make an application to be an amicus curae by Tuesday.

• Western Cape Government will respond to the application by 10h00 on Thursday. The court will then consider the matter and had down judgement on Friday.

Until then everybody has to behave themselves.

SAPS is meant to be upping its presence to ensure compliance. I am waiting to see what happened this morning.

At the same time, the taxi industry is doing a big shutdown on Wednesday relating to the other issues sketched in my piece last year:
• Impoundments
• Bylaws which they say they are going to take on review
• Golden Arrow buses working a particular route
• e-Hailing taxis

CODETA, CATA et all under the umbrella of SANTACO will be protesting in the city in front of the provincial government. This is the same day the Minister of Finance is presenting the budget vote. Last November’s stayaway – during matric exams – saw 128 000 children miss school on each of the two days of strike action.

One of the strongest education NPO’s in that space, in fact an organisation that campaigns around scholar transport, Equal Education, has only been prepared to speak to me off the record so far. They say there is little sympathy for the taxi drivers demands, and a great deal of concerns about the students, who are being disadvantaged in terms of losing out on school, as well as being intimidated by the threats that their security may be at risk. I have asked them to go back and reconsider why they don’t want to talk given that technically we are a democracy, albeit a fairly ropey one. Their view should be heard.


Further information:
Information will continue to come in this week as the court process unfolds culminating on Friday. The interdict was awarded to the MEC on March 1st 2023.

Extra Budget Items:
I will self fund an extra day of shooting to get the court engagement on on Friday 24th, in order to get more information.

Press Release:


Classroom Disruptions

In the Western Cape, there's a high-stakes contest for power and money, over the provincial transport budget, and it’s left caught in the crosfire.The local taxi industry in Cape Town is demanding a piece of the action in the City’s multi-million-rand transport tenders and they’ll stop at nothing to get it. They’re tactics are so brazen that in February, thousands of children were left stranded as taxi bosses flexed their muscles by blockading Khayelitsha, preventing scholar transport and parents alike, from transporting their children to school. Is this a symptom of a larger malaise taking over South Africa, where powerful interests use intimidation and the threat of violence, to grab tenders awarded to others? Carte Blanche investigates.

Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli



Script:


SCHOLAR TRANSPORT #6319
FINAL SCRIPT

(VO)ON THE SECOND WEEKEND IN FEBRUARY, AN ANONYMOUS VOICE MESSAGE CIRCULATED IN KHAYELITSHA, CAPE TOWN.

Sound-up from vo;
On Monday, children who do not use transport with Codeta stickers,
Will be taken out of these cars, whether going to school or creche.
If they are using transport with Codeta stickers, they will not be taken out of their transport on Monday.

(VO) IT TOLD PARENTS TO ABANDON ALL SCHOLAR TRANSPORT VEHICLES AND PUT THEIR CHILDREN IN CODETA TAXIS. THIS TOPPED THE NEWS DIARY FOR LENNY MAKASI AT THIS COMMUNITY RADIO STATION.

LENNY MAKASI
HEAD OF CURRENT AFFAIRS: ZIBONELE FM
This message had been now circulating in the social media platforms for quite a you know, when we actually picked it up as well as a radio station so we thought we might actually quickly act on that and find out though, you know, the whole truth about it.

VOICE OF ANONYMOUS DRIVER: Myself and Beep were approached by the CODETA members now,they told us we must leave now and tell your friends you mustn’t come in.

(VO) WHILE LENNY WAS BRIEFING HIS REPORTERS AT ZIBONELE FM, THE TRAFFIC ANCHOR, ZAIN JOHNSON, AT ANOTHER RADIO STATION, KFM, WAS RECEIVING URGENT MESSAGES ABOUT THE BLOCKADE FROM HIS CONTACTS ON THE GROUND. AS A SCHOLAR TRANSPORT PERMIT- HOLDER HIMSELF, HE WAS WORRIED.

ZAIN JOHNSON
TRAFFIC ANCHOR: EWN
As reports came through it was confirmed by the City of Cape Town traffic officials the taxis were actually blockading. they were told to off load their passengers, and their passengers would need to take the taxi to go to school if they wanted to go to school.

IN KHAYELITSHA REPORTERS FANNED OUT TO WORK OUT WHAT WAS GOING ON.

LENNY MAKASI
HEAD OF CURRENT AFFAIRS: ZIBONELE FM.
It was just a matter of the taxi guys stopping each and every vehicle that had a lot of people inside maybe about say three to four people and up they were just stopping everyone, and including the private school scholar transporters a…And that caused a whole lot of commotion, you know, for the community, communities community at large,

(VO) THAT MONDAY, FEBRUARY THE 13TH, 5000 CHILDREN DID NOT MAKE IT TO THEIR CLASSROOMS IN KHAYELITSHA. THE BATTLE LINES BETWEEN CODETA AND THE PROVINCIAL MEC FOR EDUCATION, DAVID MAYNIER, WERE DRAWN.

DAVID MAYNIER
MEC FOR EDUCATION, WESTERN CAPE
It's been fairly brazen. In fact, Codeta have not only released letters and press statements, but have also sort of gone on radio and done interviews where they haven't denied that they are behind the taxi blockade.

(VO) FOR FIVE DAYS, CODETA TAXIS RULED THE ROAD. AND IN KHAYELITSHA THOUSANDS OF CHLDREN STAYED AT HOME.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: At the start of the blockade, all scholar transport were told to stay away but it eventually became clear that the real target of this action were these big buses.

(VO) A HANDFUL OF BUS COMPANIES RUN SCHOLAR TRANSPORT IN KHAYELITSHA, MANY OF THEM BASED IN OTHER SUBURBS ON THE CAPE FLATS. IT’S A SERVICE CONTRACTED TO THE WESTERN CAPE EDUCATION DEPARTMENT TO THE TUNE OF R22 MILLION.

(VO) CODETA SPOKESPERSON ANDILE KHANYI SAYS THEY WANT TO BE INVOLVED.

ANDILE KHANYI
SPOKESPERSON: CODETA
We need to be part and parcel of it. We don't know how much the cake is because they never give us a full full contract of the of the of the buses. But we also want to be part and parcel of it because we're also one of the modes, is one of the modes of transport you're in Khayelitsha here as well so they must also recognise us.

(VO)IN THE HOTTEST MONTH OF THE YEAR, TEMPERATURES AROUND THIS ISSUE WERE RISING.

DAVID MAYNIER
MEC FOR EDUCATION, WESTERN CAPE
I saw kids walking to school, struggling to get to school on time in the heat. I'm extremely emotional and angry about this issue. I am also a parent. And I'm absolutely outraged that the taxi associations, as I've said,would take up to 5000 children hostage in order just simply to extort money from the state here in the Western Cape.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: : ON DAY FIVE OF THE BLOCKADE, THE MEC FOUGHT BACK. HE LAID A CRIMINAL CHARGE AGAINST CODETA AND APPLIED FOR AN URGENT INTERDICT AT THE HIGH COURT.

(VO)IN COURT, CODETA DENIED IT WAS BEHIND THE BLOCKADE.

(VO)AND IT FOUND SUPPORT FROM THE KHAYELITSHA SCHOOL GOVERNING BODIES ASSOCIATION WHICH ADDED ITS VOICE AS A FRIEND OF THE COURT. THE KSGBA IS A VOLUNTARY BODY, WHICH HAS AN EYE ON OTHER EDUCATION SECTOR CONTRACTS. ITS CHAIR IS LULAMILE MQIKELA.

LULAMILE MQIKELA
CHAIRMAN: KSGBA
Transport, nutrition, books, cleaning material and security, all the businesses taking place in their schools.

(VO)CODETA’S TAXI BOSSES LEFT THE COURT WITH PRIVATE SECURITY. GUARDS FROM KUWAIT RISK MANAGEMENT ALSO PATROL CODETA’S HEAD OFFICE AT THE KUWAIT TAXI RANK, ALWAYS AT THE READY.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: The security is run by Kuwait Risk Management? That's looking after your bosses or companies?

ANDILE KHANYI: Yes, that Is that a security company

MACFARLANE MOLELI: Now, it's discomforting for a parent to see so many guns and yet it's the same organisation that wants to take kids to school.

ANDILE KHANYI
SPOKESPERSON: CODETA
No, it is it is the safety of our organisations as well. This is a company this is a legal company and it is registered. This is a company that is also under CODETA They cannot just shoot anyone, it doesn't mean when you do have a gun, you will shoot anyone, but it is your own safety and his own protection. You cannot ask just show a gun in public if you are not security or not police or you're not bodyguard. So those are our security and are legally to be here at the rank.

(VO)AT ZIBONELE FM, COMMUNITY MEMBERS HAD BEEN PHONING IN WITH THEIR REACTIONS. LENNY MAKASI TOOK SOME OF THOSE CALLS.

LENNY MAKASI
HEAD OF CURRENT AFFAIRS: ZIBONELE FM
This one community member phoned in and said, Listen, yeah, I saw that the taxi bosses and the taxi guys were involved. I didn't even leave my house because I was afraid there might be a shooting and stuff. So most people did not even want to go on the streets, you know, people afraid of going to the shops as well, because they didn't know how this was going to play out at the end.

(VO)CAPE TOWN HAS A LONG HISTORY OF TAXI-RELATED VIOLENCE - TURF WARS OVER TRANSPORT ROUTES ARE COMMON PLACE, MANY LIVES HAVE BEEN LOST IN THE CROSS-FIRE. AND NOW SCHOOL-CHILDREN WERE IN THE MIX.

LENNY MAKASI
HEAD OF CURRENT AFFAIRS: ZIBONELE FM
Ninety-eight per cent of the people that phoned in and sent messages, they were totally against the taxi industry, totally against the taxi industry, you know,... yeah, those people are dangerous, those people they can do whatever, those people are mafias. So those were the sort of messages that we got.

(VO) MANY PEOPLE WHO WE APPROACHED IN THE COMMUNITY WERE TOO AFRAID TO TALK ON CAMERA FOR FEAR OF REPRISALS.

(VO)BUT WE FOLLOWED UP WITH THE CODETA SUPPORTERS, THE KHAYELITSHA SCHOOL GOVERNING BODIES ASSOCIATION WHICH WE FOUND TUCKED AWAY IN THIS BUILDING NEAR THE RADIO STATION.
THEIR CHAIR, LULAMILE MQUIKELA, ARGUES CODETA’s CASE.

LULAMILE MQIKELA
CHAIRMAN: KSGBA
Codeta are a part of this community. They are our uncles, our aunts, our brothers and sisters and our homeboys. So we support that they should be given opportunity to participate in the transportation of our children.

(VO)TO SHIFT THE DEADLOCK, THE KSGBA WANTS TO NEGOTIATE A NEW PARTNERSHIP AND CONTRACTING MODEL FOR ALL PROCUREMENT FOR KHAYELITSHA SCHOOLS.

LULAMILE MQIKELA
CHAIRMAN: KSGBA
We said the department on the first of April, we would like the department to ensure that the company which is supplying our schools with food, we will identify the local truck owners to transport the food from them to our institutions, as a way of creating locally, economic empowerment.

MACFARLANE MOLELI So ideally what you saying is that local businesses must be given opportunities first by the schools that are in Khayelitsha.

LULAMILE MQIKELA: Yes,

MACFARLANE MOLELI: They must then plough back into the schools?

LULAMILE MQIKELA: Exactly we want to use the recommendation power, we must recommend, that this business must be considered for contract after we have agreed with a principle of a contributing to the school.

(VO)THE MEC FOR EDUCATION UNTIL NOW HAS REFUSED TO ENGAGE WITH THIS DISCUSSION - OR ENTERTAIN CODETA’S CALLS FOR A DIFFERENT WAY OF DOING BUSINESS.

DAVID MAYNIER
MEC FOR EDUCATION, WESTERN CAPE
What CODETA apparently wants is under the guise of a partnership, they want us to circumvent a competitive bidding process, which of course, is prescribed in law and simply award them a learner transport contracts, which is illegal, and we simply could not agree to that, because this is not a mafia state here in the Western Cape.

ANDILE KHANYI
SPOKESPERSON: CODETA
Those allegations were coming from the MEC which we are very, very, very disappointed because he never met with us. Not even a single day. But we heard about gross, extortion, all those things. Those are only pure allegations which we will not accept as the taxi industry.

(VO) ON WEDNESDAY, THE HIGH COURT AWARDED THE MEC HIS INTERDICT, INSTRUCTING CODETA NOT TO OBSTRUCT OR INTERFERE WITH SCHOLAR TRANSPORT.

(VO) THIS WEEK BIG BUSES HAD SPECIAL POLICE ESCORTS. SPEAKING ON CONDITION OF ANONYMITY, THIS BUS OWNER SAYS THE OPERATORS COMPLY WITH STRICT REGULATIONS TO WIN THEIR CONTRACTS.

BUSINESSMAN: SCHOLAR TRANSPORT
By law, each vehicle, each bus will need to be road-worthied every six months, that is the normal law, with Western Cape Education Department they actually request that you road-worthy your vehicles another two times. So basically, it's four times a year. Yeah, and I don't think in that way, you can actually cut short cuts, you know, a lot of the vehicles might be old, but they are safe, and they are in roadworthy condition.

(VO) DESPITE BEING A LEGITIMATE TRADER, THE BUSINESSMAN PREFERS NOT TO REVEAL HIS IDENTITY - THE TRANSPORT TENDERS ARE UP FOR RENEWAL LATER THIS YEAR.

BUSINESSMAN: SCHOLAR TRANSPORT
The drivers are scared. You know, not only the drivers but supply chain as well. You know, they are scared, all that we want is peace

(VO) THE BLOCKADE HAS LEFT THE SCHOLAR TRANSPORT SECTOR UNEASY, AFTER IT SO DRAMATICALLY DISRUPTED THE FIRST TERM OF 2023.

ZAIN JOHNSON
TRAFFIC ANCHOR: EWN
Your bottom line here is education, it’s about getting children from home to school safely. And the taxi industry and the taxi fraternity wants to interrupt that.

PROMOS

PROMO 11 SECONDS

ZAIN JOHNSON
Your bottom line here is education. It's about getting children from home to school safely. And the taxi industry … wants to interrupt that.

PROMO ONE:
(VO) BATTLELINES ARE DRAWN BETWEEN A CAPE TOWN TAXI ASSOCIATION AND THE STATE OVER WHO SHOULD TAKE KIDS TO SCHOOL

DAVID MAYNIER
MEC FOR EDUCATION, WESTERN CAPE
In what world does a taxi association, essentially take 5000 kids hostage, put a gun to my head, and then demand that learner contracts be awarded to a Taxi Association. It's essentially the mafia state.

PROMO TWO:

(VO) TAXI DRIVERS OFFLOAD SCHOOL CHILDREN FROM SUBSIDISED SCHOOL TRANSPORT SO THAT THEY CAN GET A PIECE OF THE PIE
ANDILE KHANYI
We need to be part and parcel of it ,we're also one of the modes…of transport here in Khayelitsha as well so they must also recognise us.

LENNY MAKASI
Most of the people didn’t even want to go on the streets, you know, because they didn’t know how this was going to play out at the end.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We find out why the taxi bosses are holding school children to ransom to get transport tenders
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The disconnect between the demands of the local taxi industry in Cape Town, and the desires of the upwardly mobile Khayelitsha community to educate their children is stark. And while the scholar transport blockade can be examined on it's own as a high-stakes contest for power over the provincial transport budget, it is also a symptom of the larger malaise in South Africa, where criminal elements target and extort industries for their own gain, and undermine the rule of law, hastening South Africa's slide to a mafia state. We unpack how the Western Cape government is attempting to block CODETA as it muscles in on a R21 million scholar transport budget. The authorities use the weapons they know how to wield, namely the courts, while CODETA stands it's ground using protest and the threat of violence to make it's point, and gain ground. The school-children, the parents, the teachers and headmasters as well as the businesses who legitimately run kids to and from school are caught in the crossfire.
metadata.Summary: In the week of 13-17th February, taxi bosses flexed their muscles by blockading Khayelitsha so that thousands of children could not get to school on dedicated scholar transport. The following week, the matter is in court for an adjudication of a dispute which the WCED calls extortion, and the taxi association in question, CODETA, believes is a fair form of protest. While CODETA’s primary target was transport which was running on Western Cape Education tenders, the school blockade also affected local lift clubs, private community-based scholar transport systems that were paid for parents, and parents in private cars trying to get their kids to school. The numbers of children at home daily last week varied from 5000 to 2500. This was the biggest blockade but other blockades have been taking place for weeks on a smaller scale in other areas. CODETA shifted its response on Thursday week back to only the tender-based transport, allowing the minnows through the net. So 2854 learners on four WCED contracted Learner Transport Scheme routes in Khayelitsha had to stay at home. The value of those tenders are R21,7 million and it appears that the main beneficiaries are among others two companies – SWARTZ and ALFREDs. CODETA spokesperson told me they were not extortionists, but they wanted a piece of the cake. He said the buses were old and unsafe, and the children would be safer transported in taxis. In statements they have called the MEC racist for not engaging with them during the blockade. • The MEC refused to talk to CODETA while the blockade was ongoing, and took them to court instead, with an urgent interdict on Friday. CODETA and the provincial government signed an agreement endorsed by the court to proceed as follows: • CODETA will deliver its answering affidavit to the main application by Tuesday. • The Khayelitsha School Governing Body Association will make an application to be an amicus curae by Tuesday. • Western Cape Government will respond to the application by 10h00 on Thursday. The court will then consider the matter and had down judgement on Friday. Until then everybody has to behave themselves. SAPS is meant to be upping its presence to ensure compliance. I am waiting to see what happened this morning. At the same time, the taxi industry is doing a big shutdown on Wednesday relating to the other issues sketched in my piece last year: • Impoundments • Bylaws which they say they are going to take on review • Golden Arrow buses working a particular route • e-Hailing taxis CODETA, CATA et all under the umbrella of SANTACO will be protesting in the city in front of the provincial government. This is the same day the Minister of Finance is presenting the budget vote. Last November’s stayaway – during matric exams – saw 128 000 children miss school on each of the two days of strike action. One of the strongest education NPO’s in that space, in fact an organisation that campaigns around scholar transport, Equal Education, has only been prepared to speak to me off the record so far. They say there is little sympathy for the taxi drivers demands, and a great deal of concerns about the students, who are being disadvantaged in terms of losing out on school, as well as being intimidated by the threats that their security may be at risk. I have asked them to go back and reconsider why they don’t want to talk given that technically we are a democracy, albeit a fairly ropey one. Their view should be heard.
metadata.Further information: Information will continue to come in this week as the court process unfolds culminating on Friday. The interdict was awarded to the MEC on March 1st 2023.
